Forecasting bypass transition on one plane of a boundary layer

DNS u′ · plane y = 0.506 · x 300–500, z 0–120t = 518.75

The flow above starts laminar on the left, with long streaks, and breaks into turbulence on the right. We asked how far ahead this plane can be forecast, and whether physics plus a small neural network beats purely data-driven models.

Data

One plane, 1000 snapshots

We use the transitional boundary-layer DNS from the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database. A wall-parallel plane just above the wall is sampled on a 64 × 64 grid every 0.25 time units. The state is the streamwise and spanwise velocity fluctuation, u′ and w′.

Training, validation and test are chronological: the models never see the future. All errors are relative L2 of the fluctuation field, ‖q′ − q̂′‖ / ‖q′‖, so 100 % is no better than predicting the mean.

DatasetJHTDB transition_bl
Main gridx 300–500, z 0–120, dx 3.17, dz 1.90
Snapshots1000, t 300.00–549.75, Δt 0.25
Split700 / 150 / 150 chronological
Fine patchx 400–419.2, z 0–7.56, dx 0.305, dz 0.12; 400 consecutive snapshots + exact NS terms
Convection speedU_c ≈ 0.56 (u), 0.62 (w)
Diagnosis

The flow forgets in about six time units

Before building models we measured what is predictable. Copying the last snapshot already gives 9.9 % error one step ahead, so DMD's 1.14 % one-step error is real skill. But correlation with the starting field falls to 0.5 after 23 steps, and 61 % of the fluctuation energy sits at scales of one or two grid cells that decorrelate fastest.

So a 100-step (25 t.u.) forecast runs four times longer than the flow's memory. We judge models by valid time, large-scale error and pattern correlation, not only by full-field error at the end.

Steps until correlation < 0.523 (5.75 t.u.)
Energy at small scales (Gaussian σ = 1.5 cells)61 %

Forecasting

Physics carries the flow, a CNN corrects it

Our proposed model slides the recent history downstream at the measured convection speed, fits POD + DMD in that moving frame, and lets a 23k-parameter convolutional network correct each forecast step in one shot. Adaptive DMD covers the first four steps, where it is most accurate.

The baselines from our Stage 1 plan are adaptive DMD and linear prediction, both refitted at every forecast origin on the last 200 snapshots in a local POD basis. Press play to watch the proposed model and both baselines against the DNS from test origin 875.

u′red = faster than mean, blue = slower

Full-field error (%)

Large-scale error (%)

Linear prediction forecasts each local POD coefficient from its own last 8 values (autocorrelation method, which is always stable). Both baselines keep the right patterns for a few steps, then fade and smear them in place, ending near 93–94 % full-field error. The proposed model keeps the large structures much longer but loses the fine speckle, which is unpredictable at this grid.

The proposed model moves the flow more rigidly than the flow moves itself

We correlated each forecast frame with the first frame slid downstream at the convection speed. A value of 1 means the forecast only translates. The DNS falls to 0.60 by 25 t.u. because streaks break up and turbulent spots grow. The proposed model stays at 0.74: it is built around sliding, so it under-predicts this change of shape. This is also why it loses turbulent spots after about 40 steps.

Slide check, origin 8755 t.u.12.5 t.u.25 t.u.
Fair comparison

Beating DMD is not enough: simple references check the claim

Against our adaptive DMD baseline, the proposed model cuts large-scale error at 25 t.u. from 67 % to 40 % on average over 11 test origins. We also checked two forecasts that need no model at all, because an examiner could try them: copy the last snapshot (persistence), and slide it downstream at the convection speed (Taylor's frozen turbulence). Both beat adaptive DMD on large scales. Against the slide, our model ties up to about step 25 and then leads by 4–8 points, with a higher pattern correlation throughout. So the gain over DMD is large, but most of it comes from moving with the flow.

Compression

No fixed basis carries over to later times

A POD basis fitted on the training period captures 100 % of training energy by rank 512, yet still misses 91 % of the test fluctuation. The CNN autoencoder lands in the same place. The flow keeps producing structures the training period never contained.

A causal moving-window POD, refitted on the last 200 snapshots, reaches 4.2 % at rank 64. That is why our forecasters work in a local, adaptive basis.

Test reconstruction error (%), log scale, against rank or latent size

Physics

Split the momentum equation into what the plane can see and what it cannot

On a wall-parallel plane, the streamwise momentum equation has two parts. In-plane advection can be computed from u and w on the plane. The rest depends on flow above and below it: wall-normal transport, pressure and viscous diffusion in y. We call that the hidden term and learn it with a CNN that sees only u and w, the closure.

∂u/∂t = [ −u ∂u/∂x − w ∂u/∂z ] + [ −v ∂u/∂y − ∂p/∂x + ν∇²u ]
seen: finite differences on the plane    hidden: learned closure h(u, w)

The main grid is too coarse for this. Neighbouring points across the streaks correlate only 0.27, so finite-difference slopes are about 100 % wrong. On a fine patch near the DNS spacing they are 11–15 % off. There, physics alone predicts ∂u/∂t with 28.2 % error, a linear closure with 28.0 %, and the CNN closure with 21.7 %. The CNN explains about 57 % of the hidden term's variance.

Learned-closure simulator

Stepping the learned equation forward

We integrate the equation in time on the fine patch with RK4. Fluid enters the patch through its edges, so a frame around it is fed from the DNS, and only the interior inside the dashed box is scored. The oracle uses the exact hidden term from the database. It is unusable in practice but shows the best any closure could do with this solver.

Memory closure trained through the solver (step 12b)18.0 %36.9 %75.4 %80 / 59–65 / 12–28 % (2 seeds)

Gap closed = (physics-only error − model error) / (physics-only error − oracle error). The oracle stays near 32 % after 10 t.u., so numerics are not the bottleneck. A closure that sees only the current snapshot plateaus at 47 % of the gap after 2.5 t.u., whatever the training. Giving it memory changes that: the plane's last two snapshots reveal how the flow above and below has been acting on it. That memory closure diverges unless it is trained through the solver on its own rollouts; trained that way, it closes 80 % of the gap at 2.5 t.u. in both of two independent training runs, 59–65 % at 5 t.u., and stays stable for all 40 steps.

Making the simulator stable took 3rd-order upwind advection and a soft sponge frame. With central differences every model diverged within 15–27 steps, the oracle included. Values in the table are read from figures to about ±1 point; the player shows one start.

Two models, two questions

The forecaster and the closure are not competitors

The forecaster predicts the whole window for 25 t.u. with no help from the DNS after the start. The memory closure runs on a small fine patch, receives the true flow at its edges, and tests whether the physics the plane cannot see can be learned. Their numbers are not directly comparable.

Proposed forecasterMemory closure
QuestionHow far ahead can the plane be forecast?Can a network learn what the plane cannot see?
DomainFull window, 64 × 64 (x 300–500)Fine patch, 19.2 × 7.56 (dx 0.305)
Physics usedConvection at Uc (moving frame)Momentum equation, in-plane terms computed exactly
What is learnedCNN correction of the DMD forecastHidden term from q(t) and its recent history
DNS input after the startNone: a free forecastBoundary frame at every substep
Horizon25 t.u. (100 steps)10 t.u. (40 steps)
Compared againstAdaptive DMD, linear predictionPhysics alone, oracle
Headline result40.5 % vs 67.3 % large-scale error80 % of the gap closed at 2.5 t.u.
Main limitationSlides too rigidly; no new spotsNeeds fine-grid slopes and DNS boundaries; fades by 10 t.u.

The closure is not used as the forecaster: it needs accurate slopes, which the 64 × 64 grid lacks (98.8 % tendency error), and it is fed the DNS at its edges. Together they tell one story: the forecaster is the best prediction of the plane, and the closure is the route to forecasts that create new spots instead of sliding them.

Transition

Where the boundary layer becomes turbulent

Averaging JHTDB profiles over the span and over time gives the skin friction and shape factor along the plate. Skin friction dips below its laminar trend, then jumps onto the turbulent correlation. Transition starts at Reθ ≈ 324–347, is half complete at Reθ ≈ 428 and ends at Reθ ≈ 643, where Cf peaks. Our 64 × 64 window, x 300–500, sees the second half of transition and the young turbulent layer.

Skin friction Cf against Reθ (log–log); shaded: transition, Reθ 324–643

Shape factor H and intermittency γ along the plate

MarkerxReθ
Onset: Cf minimum225324
Onset: intermittency γ = 0.1263347
Midpoint: γ = 0.5329428
End: Cf maximum450643

Reθ = 1469 and θ = 1.82 at x = 950 agree with the database documentation (1502 and 1.88 at x = 1000), which places the transitional region around x ≈ 350. Upstream of onset, Cf already rises above the laminar value and H falls below 2.59: free-stream turbulence (Tu ≈ 3 %) drives streaks before any spot appears. Intermittency uses single points 7.5 apart in z, so it plateaus at 0.86; the Cf peak marks the end of transition. Downstream, the mean profile follows the log law with κ = 0.41 and B = 5.0.

Skin friction from the plane

What the forecasts mean at the wall

Engineers care about drag, not about u′ at y = 0.506. We trained a small CNN to read the wall shear from the plane alone, using 575 snapshots of wall data at y = 0.004. On the true plane it reproduces the time-mean Cf(x) across the window almost exactly and explains about 58 % of the instantaneous wall-shear fluctuation (correlation 0.76). A linear stochastic estimate explains about 38 % (correlation 0.63). The plane sits at y⁺ ≈ 20, so it carries the streak footprint but not the smallest near-wall scales.

Feeding each forecast through the same CNN turns forecast error into skin-friction error. The CNN on the true plane sets the ceiling.

Wall shear implied by …Wall shear, 5 t.u.Wall shear, 25 t.u.Span-mean Cf, 5 t.u.Span-mean Cf, 25 t.u.

Adaptive DMD74.5 %90.1 %49.6 %79.9 %
Linear prediction80.3 %90.1 %52.6 %91.0 %

Relative L2 error of the fluctuation, 11 test origins. The training-period mean Cf(x) agrees with the profile data within 2–4 %. In the test period the Cf peak sits at x ≈ 405 instead of ≈ 465: the transition zone drifts upstream, the same non-stationarity that limits every forecast at long horizons. Neither estimator recovers the spanwise wall shear.

Vorticity

The vorticity lives below the grid

The exact wall-normal vorticity ωy = ∂u/∂z − ∂w/∂x, queried from the database on a grid 5 × finer in x and 8 × finer in z, shows the physics directly: long laminar streaks upstream and between spots, and turbulent spots as patches of intense small-scale vorticity. One cell of our 64 × 64 grid, drawn for scale, contains many of these structures.

ComparisonCorrelation
Finite differences on the fine patch vs exact point values0.994
Finite differences on the 64 × 64 grid vs exact point values0.05
Finite differences on the 64 × 64 grid vs exact cell average (Stokes circulation)0.29

Even the fairest coarse target, the vorticity averaged over each cell and computed from the circulation around it, correlates only 0.29 with what the 64 × 64 velocity implies. Vorticity is therefore not a meaningful forecast target at this resolution, and we do not score it. On the large-scale shear the grid does resolve, the forecasts rank as everywhere else: at 25 t.u. the proposed model has 56 % error and correlation 0.84, against 76–78 % and 0.64–0.67 for the baselines.

Resolution test

Does a finer grid help the forecaster?

Downloading the whole window at fine resolution would take about 160,000 requests (roughly 9 days). First we ran the full proposed pipeline on the fine patch at four grid spacings, retraining the CNN on each, and scored every grid on the same 8 × 8 physical points. The patch is only 19.2 units long, so the history is 40 snapshots and the horizon 10 t.u., and each step is scored only where the upstream flow was inside the patch at the start.

Proposed model, seeds 0 / 11 t.u.2.5 t.u.5 t.u.10 t.u.
1× (dx 0.30)17 / 17 %28 / 28 %53 / 53 %78 / 76 %
2× (dx 0.61)23 / 23 %44 / 45 %61 / 61 %76 / 77 %
4× (dx 1.22)34 / 34 %47 / 47 %69 / 69 %80 / 80 %
8× (dx 2.44, near the main grid)45 / 45 %66 / 66 %73 / 74 %83 / 83 %

Up to about 5 t.u. resolution matters: resolved streaks can be tracked for a few time units. By 10 t.u. the grids converge to within 4–7 points, and the gap is still closing. The ranking holds at every resolution: on the finest grid at 10 t.u. the proposed model reaches 77 %, against 92 % for the Taylor slide, 90 % for moving-frame DMD and 128 % for adaptive DMD. The flow's memory, not the grid, sets the horizon, so a full fine download is not justified for 25 t.u.; a moderately finer grid (about dx 1.2, dz 0.5) is the sensible next step.

What we learned

Results that held, and results that did not

Negative results shaped the project as much as the positive ones. Each row below changed what we built next.

GRU / LSTM116 % and 120 % mean error over 100 steps: worse than predicting the mean. Replaced by physics-structured models.
Two-scale model83 % mean, worse than every baseline. Kept the scale split as a metric only.
Physics CNN, main grid98.8 % tendency error: the slopes are not in a 64 × 64 grid. Moved the physics to a fine patch.
Finer gridRerunning the full proposed model on the fine patch at four spacings: up to 37 points better at 2.5 t.u., within 4–7 points by 10 t.u. A full fine download (~9 days) is not justified for a 25 t.u. horizon.
Vorticity targetFinite differences on the 64 × 64 grid correlate 0.05 with the exact vorticity, 0.29 with its cell average. Dropped as a forecast metric; kept wall shear instead.
Wall shear from the planeA CNN explains 58 % of the wall-shear fluctuation from the plane alone, so forecasts can be scored in drag terms.
Training on rolloutsNo gain for a closure without memory. Essential for a closure with memory, which otherwise feeds on its own output and diverges.
Closure with memoryThe last two snapshots cut the closure error from 0.70 to 0.23. Trained through the solver, this becomes the best simulator in the study. With true history it even beats the exact-physics oracle, because it also corrects the solver’s own discretisation error.
Future scope

Where this goes next

Each direction answers a limitation we measured.

Create new spotsA generative or stochastic correction that learns streak break-up and spot growth, so forecasts stop merely sliding (slide check 0.74 vs 0.60 for the DNS).
More planesSeveral wall-normal planes, so wall-normal transport v ∂u/∂y can be modelled directly instead of inferred from one plane's memory.
Closure-driven forecasterRun the memory closure over the whole window on a moderately finer grid (about dx 1.2, dz 0.5, roughly 10,000 requests), which the resolution test shows is enough.
Drifting transitionOnline re-centring of the mean field and longer records: the Cf peak moves from x ≈ 465 to 405 between training and test.
Stronger evidenceMore seeds, test origins, planes and Reynolds numbers, with uncertainty bands on every forecast.
